title: The Great Automatic Grammatizator
tagline: Roald Dahl's witty speculative story about a machine that can produce stories and the human fears behind the idea of becoming unnecessary to one's own craft.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material and original practice questions written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ISC Class XI English Literature (Paper 2) syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). 'The Great Automatic Grammatizator' by Roald Dahl is named only because it is listed among the prescribed short stories in the ISC Class XI prescribed texts. BoardPrep does not reproduce the text of the story or any CISCE examination question; the explanations and practice questions here are original and are meant to support study of the prescribed story, not to replace reading it.

overview.intro: 'The Great Automatic Grammatizator' is one of the five prescribed short stories for ISC Class XI English Literature. The story imagines a machine that can write stories with astonishing speed, and it uses that invention to ask a sharply comic question: what happens when a human skill can be replaced by a machine, and what do the people whose skill is threatened try to do about it? Beneath its entertaining surface, the story is about jealousy, fear of redundancy, reputation and the uneasy relationship between human creativity and mechanical imitation.

facts.label: Core ideas
facts.value: Invention and imitation; human skill versus machine; fear of being replaced; the comedy of ambition; the way jealousy can shape a response to an innovation

learningOutcomes: Follow the central idea of the machine and the reaction to it.
Explain why the story is both comic and unsettling.
Discuss the human motives revealed by the response to the invention.
Identify the story's interest in skill, originality and redundancy.
Support observations with brief reference to the story.

blocks.text: The story begins with an invention that sounds almost absurd for its ambition: a machine that can produce stories automatically. The comic energy comes from the gap between the ordinary idea of writing, which we usually think of as intensely human, and the mechanical idea of a device that can churn out narratives. The invention matters because it raises a question many readers recognise even before the plot develops: if a machine can do what a person does, what becomes of the person?

items: The machine is the central invention of the story.
It turns a human activity into something that can be automated.
The story uses invention to create both humour and unease.
The plot grows out of how people respond to the machine, not only from the machine itself.

items.text: A reader might think the story is simply about a clever gadget. A better reading notices that the gadget is a way of testing motives: once a machine seems capable of doing the work, people's defenses and desires become visible.
items.note: The invention is a plot device but also a way of exposing character.

learn.title: Human ambition and the fear of being left behind

blocks.text: One of the story's important movements is the reaction of the people who care about writing and about being recognised as writers. The machine is not just an amusing novelty; it threatens the fragile world of reputations, practice and personal achievement. The story is sharpest when it shows how jealousy and insecurity can shape a person's judgment. In that sense, it is almost as much about human weakness as about technology.

items: The story presents a human fear of being made unnecessary.
Reputation and professional pride matter to the characters who react strongly.
Jealousy can turn an invention into a personal crisis.
The comedy is darkened by the vulnerability it exposes.

items.text: If the story were only about a machine, it would be a simple fable. Its deeper interest lies in the way the characters' fears make them behave in ways that reveal more about them than about the machine.
items.note: The human response is where the morality and the humour meet.

learn.title: Why the story is funny and disturbing at once

blocks.text: Dahl often writes in a way that blends comedy with a sharp edge. Here, the exaggeration of the machine and the speed of the events give the story a comic lift, but the underlying idea is uncomfortable: human value can feel threatened when something else appears to do the same work more efficiently. That mixture is part of what makes the story memorable. The reader laughs at the invention and then has to think about what the invention implies.

items: The story is comic in tone but serious in implication.
It exaggerates for effect without losing its point.
The unease comes from the idea that skill can be imitated.
The reader is left to measure the difference between quantity and worth.

items.text: A surface reading may enjoy the story as a tall tale about a writing machine. A fuller reading notices that the story asks whether what can be produced quickly is the same as what is worth producing.
items.note: The best answers notice both the humour and the question behind it.

keyPoints: The story is built around a machine that can write stories automatically.
The invention raises a comic but unsettling question about human skill.
Fear of being replaced shapes the characters' response.
Jealousy and pride matter as much as the machine itself.
The story blends entertainment with a serious question about value.
Brief reference to the story supports an answer more effectively than general statements about technology.
examFocus: If the question asks about the machine, explain what it represents as well as what it does.
A strong answer notices the comic tone and the underlying anxiety.
Do not write only a general 'machines are useful or dangerous' essay; keep the answer tied to the story's characters and situation.

vocabulary.meaning: A new device, method or creation, often clever or original.
Copying something made by another source or process.
The state of no longer being needed for a particular purpose.
A strong desire to achieve or be recognised.
The feeling that arises when one fears being outdone or replaced.
Writing that uses humour or exaggeration to criticise or expose folly.

questions.prompt: The central invention in the story is a machine that can:
questions.explanation: The story's plot turns on a machine built to write stories.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking the machine's purpose is only to do ordinary office work.

questions.prompt: Beneath its comic surface, the story is mainly concerned with:
options: Fear of being replaced and the value of human skill
questions.answer: Fear of being replaced and the value of human skill
questions.explanation: The story uses the machine to explore how people react when skill seems threatened.
questions.commonMistake: Treating the story as only a light humorous fantasy with no deeper point.

questions.prompt: Why does the machine cause anxiety for the people whose work is tied to writing?
questions.answer: Because if a machine can produce stories quickly, the special value of human effort, originality and reputation may seem threatened, and that raises the fear of being made unnecessary.
questions.explanation: The tension comes from the possible loss of skill and status, not just from novelty.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the anxiety is only about the machine being unusually clever.

questions.prompt: What does the story suggest about jealousy in the face of a new invention?
questions.answer: Jealousy can make people resist or misunderstand an invention because they are worried about their own position, not only because they have judged the invention on its merits.
questions.explanation: The story connects the response to the machine with personal insecurity.
questions.commonMistake: Treating the characters' reaction as purely rational or purely foolish.

questions.prompt: Discuss how the story blends comedy with a serious question about human creativity.
questions.answer: The story is funny because it presents an exaggerated machine that seems to turn writing into a mechanical output, and that exaggeration is entertaining in itself. At the same time, it raises a serious question: if a machine can imitate what a writer does, what is left for the writer to claim as uniquely valuable? The comedy draws the reader in, but the deeper effect comes from the unease behind it, where ambition, jealousy and the fear of redundancy make the invention feel threatening as well as amusing.
questions.explanation: A good answer notices the mixture of humour and anxiety and connects both to the central invention.
questions.commonMistake: Summarising the plot without discussing the tension between comedy and concern.
